en: So now with all of that out of the way,
let's dive into the first important concept
I wanna cover in this section. And that's
the difference between
real objects and data structures.
Though I also wanna already make it clear
that both terms,
real objects and data structures, are
made-up terms. These are not official terms
you will find anywhere, but this is simply a
differentiation which you sometimes find out
there, which can make sense when you're
working with objects. So what is the
difference between real objects and data
structures or data containers, as we could
also call it?
A real object hides its internals, its
properties, for example, by making them
private,
and it just exposes a public API,
a couple of methods which allow you to do
various things with this object.
And with these methods, I don't just mean
getters and setters for these hidden
properties, I mean real abstractions, so
methods which do more complex things than
just setting a property and therefore acting
as a proxy.
Data containers or data structures, on the
other hand, are simple objects where the
properties and internals are made available
publicly and where we have almost no public
API besides that, almost no methods.
Therefore, real objects matter a lot if
you're following an object-oriented
programming style. And even if you don't,
some real objects could be helpful for
encapsulating and grouping logic together,
and they contain your core business logic
therefore.
On the other hand, data containers are
really just that, These are objects which
are just used to store and transport data.
For real objects, as I mentioned a couple of
seconds ago, we prefer abstractions over
concretions, which is a fancy term which
simply means that we wanna expose methods
which define a certain task that should be
done,
and then we don't care about how the object
executes this task.
Whereas a data container doesn't really have
any methods, and therefore there we just
have the concrete data which is stored
inside of it and we can utilize that data in
the places where we get access to the data
container.
So we don't tell the container to do
something as we would do it with a real
object, we just can use it however we need
to use it.
And for example, here we have a database
class which could be used to create real
objects because it's hiding its internals
and it then has a public API which abstracts
away
the internals. Connect and disconnect are
pretty high-level methods which then
internally do everything to set up a
connection or to close a connection. And we
don't know what exactly the class will do
internally if we just call these methods.
That is what abstraction means. We just
connect to a database, which is an abstract
concept, and how exactly that works is
hidden away from us and is not our business.
If we are using such a database object.
On the other hand, this UserCredentials
class here could be used to simply create a
user credentials data container.
All the data is exposed publicly, we have no
methods, and we could just use objects based
on this class to pass credentials around,
for example, for example, as a parameter to
a function or a method.
And that's the difference between real
objects and data containers. We can use
classes for both to define these objects,
but then how we use them differs.
And now of course the question is,
why does this matter at all? Why should you
care?
